headline: Planes across the U.S. stay on the ground for hours

chunks.text: On Friday, November 13, 2026, planes across the United States were told they could not {{take off}}. The U.S. agency that runs air traffic ordered a [[nationwide]] [[ground stop]], an order that keeps all [[departing]] planes on the ground. A [[communication problem]] had hit all 22 of the country's large [[air traffic control]] centers, which guide planes between airports. More than 3,500 planes were already in the air. They kept flying and {{touched down}} safely, officials said.

verbs.correct: To leave the ground and start flying
verbs.wrong: To be checked by airport workers
verbs.why: Most planes take off from this airport in the early morning. Small planes take off from short runways. On November 13, 2026, planes across the United States were told they could not take off.

verbs.correct: To land safely at the end of a flight
verbs.wrong: To fly in circles above an airport
verbs.why: Our plane usually touches down in Denver around noon. Big jets touch down gently on long runways. More than 3,500 planes kept flying and touched down at airports around the country.

chunks.text: The agency [[lifted]] the order at 8:15 p.m. Eastern time, more than four hours after it began. In all, more than 4,000 flights were canceled and more than 10,000 were {{held up}}, according to a [[flight-tracking website]]. A [[travel data company]] said about 1.5 million people were [[stranded]]. Some airports {{ran out of}} space to park planes. Travelers {{lined up}} at [[baggage counters]] to find their bags. Others {{waited out}} the delays on airport floors.

verbs.correct: To make something late; to delay it
verbs.why: Heavy traffic often holds up the morning buses. Bad weather sometimes holds up mail delivery. More than 10,000 flights were held up, according to a flight-tracking website.

verbs.correct: To use all of something so none is left
verbs.wrong: To share something with other places
verbs.why: Small stores often run out of bread by noon. We always run out of milk on Sundays. Some airports ran out of space to park planes during the ground stop.

verbs.correct: To form a line with other people
verbs.why: Children line up at the door before lunch. Fans line up outside the stadium for tickets. At some airports, travelers lined up at baggage counters to find their bags.

verbs.correct: To wait until something bad ends
verbs.wrong: To demand a refund for a delay
verbs.why: Hikers wait out the storm inside a small cabin. Many drivers wait out the heavy snow at a rest stop. Some travelers waited out the delays on airport floors.

chunks.text: The transportation secretary blamed the country's [[aging]] air traffic control system. He said some old equipment {{broke down}}. He said [[routers]], machines that pass data between computers, got [[overloaded]] with data. Because of that, officials stopped departing flights for safety. The homeland security secretary said there was no sign of a [[cyberattack]], an attack by computer hackers. But he would not {{rule out}} anything yet.

verbs.correct: To stop working, like a machine
verbs.wrong: To be moved to a new building
verbs.why: Old copy machines often break down at the worst time. Our washing machine breaks down every few years. The transportation secretary said some old equipment broke down on November 13.

verbs.correct: To say something is not possible
verbs.why: Doctors rule out a broken bone with an X-ray. The police rarely rule out a cause early in a case. The homeland security secretary said officials would not rule out anything yet.

chunks.text: The homeland security secretary also said new equipment added to the old system seemed to have [[overwhelmed]] it. The agency has been {{rolling out}} a new tool that uses [[artificial intelligence]] to help manage air traffic. The company behind it said its tool did not cause the stop, but officials are checking that too. Officials are still {{looking into}} what went wrong and have not {{figured out}} the [[exact cause]]. Airlines warned that delays would continue on Saturday, November 14.

verbs.correct: To start using a new product or service
verbs.wrong: To test a new product in secret
verbs.why: Phone companies roll out new apps every year. Many cities roll out new bus routes in the fall. The agency has been rolling out a new tool that uses artificial intelligence to help manage air traffic.

verbs.correct: To try to find the facts about something
verbs.wrong: To share the facts with the public
verbs.why: The school looks into every complaint from parents. Insurance companies look into large claims. Officials are looking into what went wrong with the air traffic control system.

verbs.correct: To find the answer to a question
verbs.wrong: To write a report for others
verbs.why: Good mechanics figure out the problem with a car quickly. Most students figure out the answer after a few tries. Officials have not figured out the exact cause of the ground stop.

mainIdea.s: A communication problem in the air traffic control system kept departing planes on the ground across the U.S. for hours. Thousands of flights were canceled, and the cause is not known.
mainIdea.why: The order lasted more than four hours, about 1.5 million people were stranded, and officials have not figured out the exact cause.

mainIdea.s: A cyberattack on the air traffic control system stopped every flight in the U.S. for hours. Officials found the hackers quickly, and airlines say all flights are back to normal now.
mainIdea.why: Close, but officials said there was no sign of a cyberattack. They have not figured out the cause, and airlines warned of more delays.

mainIdea.s: The U.S. agency that runs air traffic hired thousands of new workers for its control centers. It says the extra staff will help airports handle the busy Thanksgiving travel season.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a ground stop. A communication problem kept planes from taking off, and thousands of flights were canceled or held up.

lines.text: Were you flying on Friday? Every airport in the country just stopped.
I heard. Planes couldn't {{take off}} anywhere. The whole system [[ground to a halt]].
For more than four hours. My cousin was stuck in Atlanta.
What about the planes that were already in the air?
They kept flying and {{touched down}} safely. Over 3,500 of them, the transportation secretary said.
Well, that's good. But I bet the airports were a mess.
Totally. Some of them {{ran out of}} space to park planes. My cousin {{waited out}} the delay on the floor by her gate.
Poor thing. Did she at least try to [[make the best of it]]?
She read a whole book. Then she {{lined up}} for an hour to find her bag.
So what caused it? Was it hackers?
Officials say there's no sign of that. But they won't {{rule out}} anything yet. The transportation secretary said some old equipment {{broke down}}.
Sounds like the system is [[showing its age]].
That's pretty much what he said. He called it incredibly old. Routers got overloaded, so they stopped all the flights.
Flights are moving again, but they haven't {{figured out}} the exact cause. They're still {{looking into}} it.
And the delays will probably keep going. It's [[a domino effect]]. Planes and crews are in the wrong cities now.
Right. If you're flying this weekend, you might be [[out of luck]].
I'm glad I'm driving to my sister's.

ex: Traffic ground to a halt after the snowstorm.
